Coarsened exact matching

Source: R/cem.R
cemtch.Rd

The matching of Iacus, King and Porro (2012): each covariate is coarsened into bins, the rows are grouped by their bins on every covariate at once, and only the groups (strata) holding both treated and control rows are kept, so that a later regression compares like with like without extrapolating.

Usage

cemtch(data, d, x, cut = NULL, lcut = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'cemtch'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per unit.

d

The name of the treatment column: 0 or 1 (or FALSE, TRUE).

x

The names of the covariate columns to match on.

cut

NULL or a named list: for a numeric covariate, the number of bins (a whole number from 1) or the breaks (increasing, covering its range).

lcut

The same for the coarsening on which l1 is measured.

...

Not used by print().

Value

An object of class cemtch, a list: keep (logical, the rows matched), strata (the stratum of each row, from 1; NA when not matched), w (the weights, 0 when not matched), tab (rows by group, all, matched and unmatched), l1 (before, after), nstrata (the strata kept and in all) and cut (the breaks used).

Details

A numeric covariate is cut into equal-width bins over its range, nclass.Sturges() of them unless cut gives the number of bins or the breaks (bins closed on the left, the last closed on both sides); a character, factor or logical covariate is matched exactly on its values. A kept stratum s with m_T^s treated and m_C^s control rows gives its treated rows weight 1 and its controls weight (m_T^s / m_C^s) (m_C / m_T), m_T and m_C the matched totals: with these weights the controls stand for the treated rows' distribution, and a weighted regression of the outcome on the treatment (with w as weights, on the rows of keep) estimates the effect on the treated (Iacus, King and Porro 2012, sec. 3; Blackwell et al. 2009, p. 529-531).

l1 is the multivariate imbalance L1 of Iacus, King and Porro (2011): half the sum over the cells of a coarsening of the absolute differences between the treated and the control shares of each cell, 0 for identical histograms and 1 for disjoint ones, before matching and after (with the weights). On the matching coarsening it is 0 after matching by construction, so it is measured on the coarsening of lcut, by default Scott's rule (nclass.scott() equal-width bins) for each numeric covariate.

Sampson and Winter (2018) define children with a mean blood lead level of 6 micrograms per decilitre or more as treated, match them on categorical traits of the child, the caregiver and the neighbourhood (Blackwell et al. 2009), report L1 falling "from .71 to nearly 0" (p. 283), and then fit ordinary least squares on the matched sample; they assess mediators (impulsivity, anxiety) by adding them to that regression (p. 289).

Talayero et al. (2023) review seventeen studies of measured lead (blood, bone or dentine) and later delinquent or criminal behaviour, rating each for confounding, and find "limited data at the individual level" (abstract).

References

Iacus, S. M., King, G. and Porro, G. (2012). Causal inference without balance checking: coarsened exact matching. Political Analysis, 20, 1-24. doi:10.1093/pan/mpr013

Iacus, S. M., King, G. and Porro, G. (2011). Multivariate matching methods that are monotonic imbalance bounding. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 106, 345-361. doi:10.1198/jasa.2011.tm09599

Blackwell, M., Iacus, S., King, G. and Porro, G. (2009). cem: coarsened exact matching in Stata. The Stata Journal, 9, 524-546.

Sampson, R. J. and Winter, A. S. (2018). Poisoned development: assessing childhood lead exposure as a cause of crime in a birth cohort followed through adolescence. Criminology, 56(2), 269-301. doi:10.1111/1745-9125.12171

Talayero, M. J., Robbins, C. R., Smith, E. R. and Santos-Burgoa, C. (2023). The association between lead exposure and crime: a systematic review. PLOS Global Public Health, 3(8), e0002177. doi:10.1371/journal.pgph.0002177

Examples

set.seed(2)
n <- 300
d <- data.frame(pov = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4), age = runif(n, 14, 18))
d$lead <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + 1.5 * d$pov))
d$y <- 0.5 * d$lead + d$pov + 0.2 * d$age + rnorm(n)
m <- cemtch(d, "lead", c("pov", "age"), cut = list(age = 4))
m
#> cemtch: coarsened exact matching, 8 of 8 strata kept
#>           control treated
#> all           177     123
#> matched       177     123
#> unmatched       0       0
#> L1 imbalance: 0.416 before, 0.142 after
stats::lm(y ~ lead, d, weights = m$w, subset = m$keep)
#> 
#> Call:
#> stats::lm(formula = y ~ lead, data = d, subset = m$keep, weights = m$w)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)         lead  
#>      3.9217       0.5045  
#>
